newsitem.title: USA: A totally killer time at the prom sans mega-bucks.
newsitem.headline: A totally killer time at the prom sans mega-bucks.

text.p: Anyone over the age of 40 needs subtitles to understand what today's teens are talking about, but when it comes to deciphering finances involving the prom, the message is loud and clear.
The prom is the single most expensive date a teenager will ever have.
Who's going to foot the bill and how can the financial damage be kept under control?

Currently, it is not unusual for a teenaged girl to spend $1,000 on dress, hair, make-up and accessories for a night at the prom. A boy can spend hundreds of dollars for rental of a tuxedo, flowers and extras. A single prom ticket costs an average of $80.
If you live on the East Coast or West Coast you'll likely spend more money on the prom than if you live in the middle of the country.
While the emotional stakes might be high, the rules of date etiquette should not go out the window just because it's the prom. In other words, should girls pay?
"Oh absolutely. It's so retro to expect him to pay for everything," said Christina Boyle, associate editor of YM magazine.

"If you look at this as a normal date, it's less threatening." In addition to springing for one's own ticket, "A girl should feel comfortable to offer to pay for milkshakes and fries after the prom at a diner."
Boyle agrees that the prom should be primarily financed by the teens but parents have to realise "that proms certainly are expensive."
Adults can chip in for a limousine or a party bus, which is less expensive per person than a limo, and "it'll make parents more comfortable" knowing there is a designated driver.

If some teens think about the prom further ahead than March, "maybe they can take it on themselves to earn some cash, but parents should clue into the fact that kids are in school and not able to pay for everything," Boyle said.
Even at $80 a person, the prom ticket alone is but a minor part of the total night's expense. In many cases, pre- and post-prom parties are essential parts of the package, and hence, the cost.

Boyle suggests that rather than renting a hotel or banquet room for a pre-prom party as many teens feel they must, have a pre-prom party at someone's house where the host only has to "shell out money for snacky foods."
Post-prom, nix the idea of going to a club (essentially cool according to some teen magazines) and "go to a 24-hour diner or late night amusement centre or have a party at someone's house."

To keep dress prices down, Boyle said that with shopping around and comparison pricing, this year's "Emma" inspired dresses can be bought for $100 or less. While girls can spend up to $300 on gowns, with dresses by Nicole Miller, a popular designer, at the high end, YM offers the frugal solution of "a hip find from a vintage shop."
Rather than paying for pictures taken by a professional photographer, use "a disposable camera with flash for your own cool candids," the magazine offers.
Instead of renting a stretch limo, use "an uncle's convertible, with your older bro playing chauffeur."
In addition, it's totally acceptable to ask your best buds to help you do your own hair.

"You don't have to spend a ton of money on your makeup" by buying new products specifically for your big night out, Boyle said. The natural, minimal makeup look of Gwyneth Paltrow, star of the film "Emma" and finance to total babe Brad Pitt, is in, anyway.

The best way to keep prom expenses down is to get in on the planning on the ground floor. If you're a high school junior or sophomore and you're involved in making prom plans for your classmates, "you won't be bitter about the cost," Boyle said.

Have a question of solution to make your money go further? Write Judith Schoolman c/o Reuters, 199 Water Street, 10th floor, New York, N.Y. 10038, or e-mail to JUDITH.SCHOOLMAN (at)REUTERS.COM. She regrets she cannot answer letters personally but will try to address them in future columns.
